newsitem.title: UK: NatWest suffers as Markets profits slump.
newsitem.headline: NatWest suffers as Markets profits slump.

text.p: National Westminster Bank announced first half results which were slightly ahead of market expectations on Tuesday but which also showed the true extent of the collapse in profits at its NatWest Markets investment banking unit.

NatWest made 775 million pounds ($1.3 billion) from its continuing business in the first half -- five million more than it forecast in a profits warning in June. But the investment bank saw its profits slide to 58 million pounds from 219 million in the first half of last year.
NatWest chief executive Derek Wanless sought to end speculation over the group saying that what remains of NatWest Markets after last week's reorganisation was not for sale.
Asked if he intended to sell the operation, Wanless said in an interview: "No way, it's not up for sale."

He also denied that the reorganisation of the Markets unit was just a cosmetic exercise, adding it was important to remember that 10 billion pounds of capital would be removed from the area over two years.
"I'm confident now, with the new management we've got in place that they'll get the return up," he added.
Wanless said the capital would either be used in the rest of the business or, if found to be surplus, returned to shareholders, since the bank was not planning any major acquisitions.

Last Friday, NatWest appointed an insider, Konrad "Chip" Kruger as chief executive of NatWest Markets which had its financial markets businesses, including Treasury, Money Markets and Foreign Exchange, taken and put in a new segment of the main bank to be called Global Financial Markets (GFM).

GFM made a profit of 169 million pounds in the first half but the rump of NatWest Markets made a massive 111 million pounds loss including the 77 million lost in interest rate options trading which started the whole debate over NatWest's future when it was discovered in February.
Wanless admitted that at 13.4 percent, the Group's return on equity was inadequate but said the performance of its retail and commercial bank NatWest UK and of its Ulster Bank unit had been positive.
He said costs were under control with the cost to income ratio in NatWest UK dipping to 66.4 percent from 71 in the first half of last year.
"We had a very strong performance in our (credit) card business and we are doing well in corporate banking," Wanless said.

NatWest UK saw profit before tax rise by just four percent to 471 million stg before taking into account restructuring costs which were 84 percent lower than last year. Net interest income was higher but non-interest income fell.

Bad debt provisions were flat for the group at 270 million pounds with improvements at NatWest UK offset by increases at Lombard and the private banking unit Coutts which increased provisions by 17 million pounds "mainly from a single large provision in the U.S." but which otherwise had a trading surplus up 37 percent.
NatWest shares declined after the results, dropping 20 pence to stand at 850p.
